extracted.intended_audience: scholars, researchers, program officers, and others interested in grant peer review and academic evaluation processes
extracted.subtask_description: Description and analysis of customary rules, norms, and practical constraints that shape how grant peer review panels evaluate proposals—with attention to multidisciplinary panels, deliberation dynamics, and sources of bias and legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Following customary rules preserves fairness and legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the customary supra-individual rules discourages corruption and helps ensure that the best proposals are identified; these rules maintain a sense of fairness in pursuit of excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter emphasizes that adherence to customary rules both structures deliberation and generates legitimacy for the process; breaches reveal the rules most clearly. Examples include rules that bracket self-interest and respect disciplinary sovereignty. Scoring guidance: following these rules increases perceived legitimacy and credibility among panelists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context of evaluation is relational and comparative
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals are evaluated relationally, in comparison with other proposals; the universe of comparison is not stable, nor are the criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators should recognize that judgments depend on what else is in the pool and that criteria shift with the set of proposals. Anti-pattern: treating evaluation as purely intrinsic to a single proposal without reference to its competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic understanding of fairness (strategic judging)
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists support a pragmatic understanding of fairness that departs from the ideal of considering only intrinsic qualities; because many judgments are relational and conjectural, panelists think strategically about what they can realistically accomplish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers often act strategically (e.g., trading votes, prioritizing feasible wins) rather than strictly following abstract ideals. Guidance: be explicit about realistic trade-offs and the limits of what the panel can achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpersonal relationships and clientelism influence evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The influence of interpersonal relationships, including clientelism, cannot be totally eliminated because scholarly expertise is superimposed onto social networks of applicants and evaluators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that social ties and reputations shape who gets benefit of doubt. Anti-pattern: assuming social network effects are absent; mitigation requires transparency and rule enforcement but cannot fully remove influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiosyncratic evaluations are unavoidable and often universalized
rubrics_metrics.description: Idiosyncratic evaluations are almost unavoidable, yet they are usually presented in universalistic terms and folded into formal criteria of evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists should be aware that personal tastes and judgments will influence outcomes even when couched in universal language. Guidance: surface idiosyncratic bases where possible, and be cautious about re-labeling personal preferences as objective criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respecting customary deliberation rules is crucial for credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Respecting the customary rules of deliberations is crucial for accumulating credibility with co-panelists (a necessary condition for making one’s label 'stick' to a proposal) and for facilitating deliberations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be persuasive, panelists should adhere to norms (e.g., bracketing self-interest, turn-taking, disciplinary deference). Violations reduce influence and slow decision-making. Scoring implication: credibility with peers affects weight of one’s opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation is interactional and emotional, not purely cognitive
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of evaluating is an eminently interactional and emotional undertaking rather than solely a cognitive process corrupted by extra-cognitive factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels generate emotional energy and group dynamics that shape judgments. Guidance: anticipate group affect, manage emotional dynamics, and understand that feelings of legitimacy support acceptance of outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time pressures and panelist exhaustion affect decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists’ intellectual exhaustion after multi-day meetings and time pressures (e.g., flights) influence how they carry out their task and can lead to suboptimal outcomes (e.g., not distributing all fellowships).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical constraints like meeting length, scheduling, and fatigue should be accounted for when designing review processes. Anti-pattern: packing excessive deliberation into short schedules; mitigation: build in recovery time and realistic schedules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group culture (humor, inside jokes) can disrupt seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: During prolonged meetings panelists often develop a common sense of humor and group culture that may disrupt the seriousness of deliberations and make certain topics into the 'butt of the joke.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be attentive to how in-group humor or culture can marginalize topics or applicants. Guidance: moderators should manage culture to keep deliberations focused and respectful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disciplinary sovereignty affects speaking rights and deference
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule about respecting disciplinary sovereignty influences emotional management of panels and who is allowed to speak authoritatively on particular topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In multidisciplinary panels, deference to disciplinary experts helps manage disagreements; in unidisciplinary panels this rule may not apply and there may be competition to claim speaking rights. Implication: panel composition shapes norms of deference and advocacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between multidisciplinary and unidisciplinary panels
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes documented apply to multidisciplinary panels; unidisciplinary panels follow different rules — e.g., more competition to appropriate the right to speak when members are from the same discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and interpret panel behavior in light of panel composition. Guidance: anticipate different dynamics and rules depending on whether the panel is multidisciplinary or unidisciplinary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical realities (prestige-based recruitment) shape perceptions of fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Program officers consider prestige when recruiting members; more successful scholars are likelier to internalize that peer review 'works,' while those excluded may view allocation as particularistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how recruitment practices and panel composition (prestige bias) affect both actual allocation and beliefs about legitimacy. Anti-pattern: assuming uniformly shared belief in fairness across all academic constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic behaviors (horse-trading, strategic voting) are unavoidable
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategic voting, horse-trading, self-interest, and inconsistent criteria are unavoidable parts of panel decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than assuming their absence, systems should anticipate strategic behavior and design procedures (transparency, norms enforcement) to limit corrupting effects while accepting some pragmatic negotiation as part of the process.
